events.title: Mayflower Compact Signed
events.blurb: 41 male passengers of a merchant ship that had landed at the wrong spot on the Massachusetts coast — they had intended the Hudson River — signed a short agreement on the ship to govern themselves by the will of the majority until permanent civil authority could be established. The document was pragmatic, not ideological, but became a foundational text of American self-government. The Pilgrims who signed it were fleeing religious persecution in England via the Netherlands.
events.revealBlurb: November 11, 1620 (Old Style) / November 21, 1620 (New Style) — aboard the Mayflower, Cape Cod. Half the colony's 102 passengers died of scurvy and starvation the first winter. The autumn 1621 harvest feast with the Wampanoag is the ancestor of the American Thanksgiving.

events.title: Alien and Sedition Acts Signed
events.blurb: President John Adams signed four statutes that extended the residency requirement for citizenship from five to fourteen years, empowered the president to expel foreigners deemed dangerous, and made it a crime to publish "false, scandalous, and malicious" criticism of the government. The laws were aimed largely at French immigrants and Republican newspaper editors who opposed the Federalist administration.
events.revealBlurb: July 14, 1798 — Philadelphia (the Sedition Act, last of the four). Twenty-five people were arrested and ten convicted under the Sedition Act — all of them Jefferson's supporters. Jefferson himself quietly wrote the Kentucky Resolutions arguing states could nullify federal law.

events.title: Emancipation Proclamation Takes Effect
events.blurb: President Abraham Lincoln's executive order declaring freedom for all enslaved people in Confederate states in active rebellion took legal effect at the new year, transforming the character of the war from a constitutional dispute over secession into an explicit struggle over slavery. The proclamation did not free enslaved people in border states still in the Union, but it authorized the enlistment of Black men into the Union Army — eventually nearly 200,000 would serve.
events.revealBlurb: January 1, 1863 — Washington, D.C. Lincoln spent the morning shaking hundreds of hands at a White House reception; by the time he sat down to sign the Proclamation his hand trembled so badly he paused. "If my name ever goes into history it will be for this act," he said.

events.title: Scopes "Monkey Trial" Begins
events.blurb: John T. Scopes, a high school teacher in Dayton, Tennessee, went on trial for violating a state law banning the teaching of human evolution in public schools. The case — which pitted famed defense attorney Clarence Darrow against three-time presidential nominee and Christian fundamentalist William Jennings Bryan — was broadcast nationally on radio and drew journalists from across the country to the small town.
events.revealBlurb: July 10, 1925 — Dayton, Tennessee. The trial was deliberately staged by the town's businessmen to attract tourists and publicity; Scopes wasn't sure he had actually taught evolution. He was convicted and fined $100, but the verdict was overturned on a technicality. Bryan died five days after the trial ended.

events.title: January 6: U.S. Capitol Attacked
events.blurb: That morning, a mob of several thousand supporters of President Donald Trump stormed the U.S. Capitol building, breaching the chambers and offices of Congress as legislators were in the process of certifying the Electoral College results of the 2020 presidential election. The attack — the first violent breach of the Capitol since British forces burned it in 1814 — resulted in five deaths on the day and led to Trump's second impeachment.
events.revealBlurb: January 6, 2021 — Washington, D.C. Over 1,200 people were charged with crimes related to the attack, the largest criminal investigation in U.S. Justice Department history. Congress completed the electoral certification at 3:44 am the following morning. The Capitol had not been occupied by hostile forces since August 24, 1814.

events.title: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman
events.blurb: An English writer who had been educating herself in French enlightenment philosophy published a 300-page treatise arguing that women appeared inferior only because they received inferior education, and that a rational republic required the rational education of both sexes. It was attacked, praised, and influential on both sides of the Atlantic. She died five years later from complications after childbirth.
events.revealBlurb: January 1792 — Mary Wollstonecraft. The child she died giving birth to was Mary Shelley, author of Frankenstein. Her husband, William Godwin, published an honest memoir after her death that destroyed her reputation for a century.

events.title: UK Women Get the Vote
events.blurb: A British parliament, persuaded partly by the contribution of women to the wartime labour force, enfranchised women householders and university graduates aged 30 and over — extending the franchise to about 8.5 million new voters. Complete parity with men would take another decade. One of its first fruits was the election, shortly after, of a woman to the Commons, who declined to take her seat.
events.revealBlurb: February 6, 1918 — Representation of the People Act. The non-taking-her-seat member was Constance Markievicz, elected for Sinn Féin in Dublin; she refused to swear allegiance to the Crown. Women 21-29 got the vote in 1928.

events.title: Amelia Earhart Disappears
events.blurb: On the penultimate leg of an around-the-world flight at the equator, a 39-year-old American aviator and her navigator took off from a Pacific airstrip bound for a tiny coral island 4,100 kilometres away. Her final radio messages reported low fuel and inability to locate the island. A Navy search of 400,000 square kilometres of ocean found nothing. Her disappearance has launched a hundred books and at least three feature films.
events.revealBlurb: July 2, 1937 — Earhart and Fred Noonan bound for Howland Island. Prevailing theories: ran out of fuel and ditched; landed on uninhabited Nikumaroro and died of thirst; captured by the Japanese. No conclusive physical evidence exists.

events.title: Margaret Thatcher Becomes PM
events.blurb: The leader of the British Conservative Party, a grocer's daughter who had studied chemistry at Oxford and later trained as a barrister, was invited by the monarch to form a government after her party won a sweeping parliamentary majority. She became the United Kingdom's first woman prime minister and would hold the office for 11 years — the longest continuous premiership of the 20th century.
events.revealBlurb: May 4, 1979 — she took office quoting St. Francis of Assisi on the doorstep: "Where there is discord, may we bring harmony." The next decade would be anything but that. She was forced to resign by her own cabinet in November 1990.

events.title: Sally Ride in Space
events.blurb: A 32-year-old astrophysicist, riding as mission specialist aboard a space shuttle launched from a Florida coastal site, became the first American woman — and the youngest American — to reach orbit. NASA had asked her at the pre-flight press conference whether space travel would affect her reproductive organs; she answered that there was no evidence either way.
events.revealBlurb: June 18, 1983 — Space Shuttle Challenger, STS-7 mission. She flew a second mission in 1984 and was on the commission investigating the 1986 Challenger disaster that killed seven of her colleagues. She came out as a lesbian in her 2012 obituary.

events.title: Caesar Crosses the Rubicon
events.blurb: A Roman general returning from nine years of conquest in Gaul, forbidden by law from bringing his army across the small river marking the boundary of Italy proper, led a single legion across anyway — knowing the act constituted treason against the Republic. He was reportedly quoting a Greek tragedian: "the die is cast." His subsequent march on Rome ignited a four-year civil war, at the end of which he emerged as a dictator-for-life and the Republic ended in everything but name.
events.revealBlurb: January 10, 49 BCE — Julius Caesar with Legion XIII. "Alea iacta est" — "the die is cast" — is attributed to him crossing. The Rubicon itself is a small, easily missable river in northern Italy; its modern identity is still debated by historians. The phrase "crossing the Rubicon" has since become an English idiom.

events.title: Octavian Becomes Augustus
events.blurb: The Roman Senate voted Gaius Octavian a new and previously unused title — Augustus, "the revered" — along with broad military command, tribunician power for life, and control of the key frontier provinces. He kept the word "republic" in circulation and called himself only "first citizen," but every structural mechanism of one-man rule was now legally his.
events.revealBlurb: January 16, 27 BCE. Augustus lived another 41 years and died of natural causes at 75 — an almost freakish accomplishment for a Roman emperor. His last words, spoken to friends, were reportedly: "Did I play the part well? Then applaud as I exit."

events.title: Year of the Four Emperors
events.blurb: In a single calendar year, the Roman principate cycled through four rulers — Galba, Otho, Vitellius, and Vespasian — as competing legions backed their own generals in an open civil war. Vespasian, commanding troops in Judaea, won by securing Egypt's grain supply first and strangling Rome's food imports until the Senate gave in.
events.revealBlurb: 69 CE. Otho lost one battle, decided he didn't want more Romans to die for him, and stabbed himself — widely praised as his most noble act. Vitellius, who followed, spent his months in power eating. He was eventually dragged through Rome, publicly mocked, killed, and thrown in the Tiber.

events.title: Aurelian Reunifies the Empire
events.blurb: After the empire had fractured into three competing states, Emperor Aurelian defeated the Palmyrene Empire in the east — capturing its queen Zenobia — and then the breakaway Gallic Empire in the west, bringing Britain, Gaul, Spain, Syria, and Egypt back under a single ruler within five years of taking power. He then began building a massive new defensive wall around Rome itself.
events.revealBlurb: 274 CE. Queen Zenobia of Palmyra had claimed descent from Cleopatra and ruled a sophisticated court of scholars and poets while commanding legions across the Near East. After capture she was eventually settled near Tivoli and, according to some sources, married a Roman senator.

events.title: Permanent Division of the Roman Empire
events.blurb: On his deathbed in Mediolanum, Emperor Theodosius divided the empire between his two sons: eighteen-year-old Arcadius took the east with Constantinople, and ten-year-old Honorius took the west with its capital at Ravenna. No mechanism existed to reunite the two halves, and none ever did.
events.revealBlurb: January 17, 395 CE. Theodosius was the last man to rule the entire Roman Empire. His ten-year-old western heir Honorius grew up to be a notably passive emperor; later historians note that when told "Rome has fallen," he reportedly burst into tears — then relaxed when he learned it was the city, not his favourite hen, also named "Rome."

events.title: September 11 Attacks
events.blurb: Nineteen hijackers affiliated with al-Qaeda commandeered four commercial airliners on a Tuesday morning, crashing two into the twin towers of a Manhattan financial complex, one into a Pentagon wing, and one into a Pennsylvania field after passengers fought back. Both World Trade Center towers collapsed within two hours. 2,977 people died. The attacks reshaped American foreign policy, launched two wars that lasted the next two decades, and redefined commercial aviation security for a generation.
events.revealBlurb: September 11, 2001 — orchestrated by Osama bin Laden. United States entered Afghanistan in October 2001 and Iraq in March 2003. The 9/11 Memorial & Museum opened on the site in 2014; One World Trade Center, topped out in 2013, is the tallest building in the Western Hemisphere.

events.title: Britney Shaves Her Head
events.blurb: A 25-year-old American pop star walked into a Los Angeles hair salon at 8 PM, asked a stylist to shave her head completely, and when the stylist refused, picked up the electric clippers and did it herself. Paparazzi captured the scene through the salon window. Images went global within hours, becoming an emblem of a period of intensely public personal struggle — divorce, custody battles, reportage, and tabloid harassment. She would be placed under conservatorship nine months later.
events.revealBlurb: February 16, 2007 — Britney Spears at Esther's Haircutting Studio, Tarzana, CA. The conservatorship lasted 13 years, ending in November 2021 after the #FreeBritney movement. Her 2023 memoir "The Woman in Me" describes the head-shaving as a reaction to feeling over-managed and pressured by the industry.

events.title: Balloon Boy Hoax
events.blurb: A Colorado family reported that their 6-year-old son had been carried aloft in a homemade silver mylar weather balloon that had drifted off from their backyard. National news networks covered the balloon's two-hour, 80-kilometre flight live, interrupting regular programming. The balloon landed empty. The boy was found hiding in the family attic. Within a day, the father admitted the whole thing had been a publicity stunt, hoping to land the family a reality-TV show.
events.revealBlurb: October 15, 2009 — Heene family, Fort Collins, CO. The father Richard Heene was convicted of a felony and served 30 days; the mother Mayumi got misdemeanor charges. The Heenes reportedly received a pardon from Colorado governor Jared Polis in December 2020.

events.title: Kim Kardashian "Breaks the Internet"
events.blurb: A 34-year-old reality TV star and entrepreneur appeared on the cover of a magazine nude, balancing a champagne glass on her bared posterior, with a headline directly daring the internet to be broken by it. The cover image was shared widely enough that the magazine's website crashed for short periods. The photograph — shot by a French photographer who had staged similar images four decades earlier — launched weeks of commentary about sexuality, race, body image, and the limits of viral marketing.
events.revealBlurb: November 11, 2014 — Kim Kardashian on Paper magazine. Photographer Jean-Paul Goude had shot nearly identical images with other models in the 1970s and 80s, drawing accusations that he specifically emphasized and sexualized Black bodies. The cover did, in fact, briefly break the magazine's website.

events.title: David Bowie Dies
events.blurb: A 69-year-old English singer and songwriter died of liver cancer at his New York apartment, two days after releasing what turned out to be his final studio album. The album's cover art, title ("Blackstar"), and lyrics — which in retrospect clearly addressed death — had been a farewell that almost nobody had caught in real time. His decades of genre-shifting personas, starting with the glam-rock Ziggy Stardust in 1972, had made him one of the most influential musicians of the late 20th century. His death prompted an international wave of mourning.
events.revealBlurb: January 10, 2016 — David Bowie (David Robert Jones). Diagnosed 18 months earlier; kept the illness private. His final public appearance was at the premiere of his off-Broadway musical "Lazarus" in December 2015. 2016 became known as a year of many significant music deaths.

events.title: First Ether Anesthesia Demo
events.blurb: A Boston dentist administered inhaled diethyl ether vapour to a patient in the surgical amphitheatre of Massachusetts General Hospital, rendering him unconscious while a leading surgeon removed a tumour from his neck. The patient woke pain-free. The surgeon turned to the assembled observers and said, "Gentlemen, this is no humbug." Surgical anesthesia had arrived; the previous era of surgery as fast, agonizing amputations in the patient's full consciousness was ending.
events.revealBlurb: October 16, 1846 — dentist William T. G. Morton and surgeon John Collins Warren at MGH, Boston. The amphitheatre, now called the "Ether Dome," is preserved as a National Historic Landmark. Morton spent the rest of his life in failed litigation trying to collect royalties on the technique.

events.title: Nightingale at Scutari
events.blurb: A 34-year-old British nurse arrived with 38 volunteer nurses at a filthy military hospital in a former Turkish barracks outside a Bosphorus capital, where British wounded from a Crimean war were dying of typhus, cholera, and dysentery at far higher rates than from combat wounds. Her reforms — sanitation, proper food, hand-washing, laundry — cut the death rate from 42 percent to 2 percent in six months. Her subsequent statistical advocacy reshaped nursing as a profession.
events.revealBlurb: November 4, 1854 — Florence Nightingale at Scutari (now Üsküdar, Istanbul). Her nighttime rounds with an oil lamp produced the "Lady with the Lamp" sobriquet. She returned to London with chronic brucellosis, spent most of the rest of her life bedridden, and still wrote 200 books and reports. She lived to 90.

events.title: Insulin Administered to a Patient
events.blurb: A 14-year-old diabetic patient near death at a Toronto hospital received an injection of pancreatic extract prepared by two medical researchers after earlier formulations had failed due to impurities. The boy recovered, and researchers moved ward to ward injecting the remaining diabetic patients — transforming a death sentence into a manageable condition within weeks.

events.title: First Successful Organ Transplant
events.blurb: A Boston surgical team performed the first successful kidney transplant, grafting a kidney donated by a healthy 23-year-old into his identical twin, who had been dying of chronic nephritis. The donor-recipient genetic match avoided rejection in an era before immunosuppressive drugs existed. The recipient lived eight more years; the donor lived another 56. The operation established organ transplantation as a viable medical field.
events.revealBlurb: December 23, 1954 — Joseph Murray at Peter Bent Brigham Hospital, Boston. Donor: Ronald Herrick. Recipient: Richard Herrick. Murray won the 1990 Nobel Prize in Medicine. Cyclosporine, the immunosuppressive that would permit non-related transplants, was not discovered until the 1970s.

events.title: First CT Scanner
events.blurb: A British engineer at a small electronics company introduced the first clinical computed tomography scanner, which used X-ray beams and computer reconstruction to produce cross-sectional images of the inside of a patient — the first medical imaging breakthrough since the X-ray 76 years earlier. Early scans took hours and resolved only the head; within a decade the technology could produce full-body scans in minutes.
events.revealBlurb: October 1, 1971 — Godfrey Hounsfield at EMI; first clinical scan at Atkinson Morley's Hospital, Wimbledon, London. Hounsfield shared the 1979 Nobel with Allan Cormack. EMI funded the research from its Beatles albums revenue.

events.title: Euclid's Elements Written
events.blurb: A 13-book mathematical treatise organised geometry, number theory, and proportion into a rigorous deductive system built from five simple axioms and five postulates, from which hundreds of theorems were derived by logical proof alone. The work became the model for mathematical reasoning for more than two thousand years and remained a standard university textbook in parts of Europe into the twentieth century.
events.revealBlurb: c. 300 BCE — almost nothing is known about Euclid himself; even his birthdate is unknown. The Elements is the second most-printed book in history after the Bible. One of its five postulates — the parallel postulate — resisted proof for two thousand years; mathematicians who tried to derive it instead invented non-Euclidean geometry.

events.title: Photoelectric Effect Explained
events.blurb: A paper explained why shining light on a metal surface ejects electrons only when the light exceeds a threshold frequency — never for very bright low-frequency light — by proposing that light itself travels in discrete energy packets rather than continuous waves. The finding resolved a long-standing paradox and extended the quantum idea from heat radiation to light, fundamentally changing the understanding of what light is.
events.revealBlurb: June 9, 1905 — this was the paper that explicitly won Einstein the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics, not relativity. When the Nobel Committee finally awarded it (sixteen years late), they cited this discovery specifically. Einstein reportedly joked that the committee must have found relativity too controversial.

events.title: Continental Drift Hypothesis Presented
events.blurb: A German meteorologist proposed that Earth's continents were once joined in a single supercontinent that had since broken apart and drifted slowly across the ocean floor, citing the geometric fit of coastlines, matching fossil records on opposite sides of the Atlantic, and ancient glacial scour marks in tropical regions. The geological community's response was immediate and largely hostile.
events.revealBlurb: January 6, 1912 — Alfred Wegener's hypothesis was mocked at a major American geological meeting in 1926, where a speaker suggested geologists should "be instantly prepared to disregard" it. Wegener died on a Greenland expedition in 1930. The mechanism he was missing — seafloor spreading — was found by Harry Hess in the 1960s.

events.title: Plate Tectonics Theory Accepted
events.blurb: After decades of ridicule, a theory holding that Earth's crust is fractured into massive slabs drifting centimetres each year was vindicated by magnetic stripe patterns mapped on either side of mid-ocean ridges. The pattern matched predictions for seafloor spreading, explaining continental shapes, mountain ranges, and earthquake zones in a single framework.
events.revealBlurb: 1967–68 — the "plate tectonics revolution". Alfred Wegener had proposed continental drift in 1912 and been mocked for it; he died in 1930 on an expedition in Greenland. Geologists officially accepted his core idea thirty-seven years after his death.

events.title: Higgs Boson Announced
events.blurb: At a packed seminar, two independent experimental teams working at the world's largest particle accelerator announced the observation of a new particle consistent with the long-predicted Higgs boson — the quantum field excitation that gives other fundamental particles their mass. The discovery completed the standard model of particle physics, confirming a prediction made nearly fifty years earlier.
events.revealBlurb: July 4, 2012 — Peter Higgs, who had predicted the boson in 1964, was in the audience and reportedly wept. The two experiments — ATLAS and CMS — had been run in blind competition to avoid bias. Higgs and François Englert shared the Nobel Prize in Physics the following year.

events.title: Watt's Separate Condenser Patent
events.blurb: A Scottish instrument maker received a patent for a steam engine design that used a separate condenser chamber, dramatically reducing fuel consumption. Unlike earlier designs that wasted energy reheating the main cylinder on every stroke, the new engine converted roughly 75% more heat into mechanical work.

events.title: Watt's Separate Condenser
events.blurb: A 33-year-old Scottish instrument maker, repairing a model of a 50-year-old atmospheric engine for a university natural philosophy class, realized its efficiency was fatally compromised by repeatedly heating and cooling the same cylinder. His solution — a separate condensing vessel — cut fuel consumption by 75 percent. Patented four years later, the improved engine could be sited anywhere, not only beside a coal pit, and became the prime mover of 19th-century industry.
events.revealBlurb: 1765 insight; January 5, 1769 patent — James Watt. His decade-long partnership with Birmingham industrialist Matthew Boulton commercialized the engine. The unit of power is named for him. "Horsepower" was also his invention, a marketing metric.

events.title: Rocket Wins the Rainhill Trials
events.blurb: A north-west English railway company held a ten-day public competition to choose the locomotive type for its forthcoming long-distance line between two major industrial cities. Five entries competed; three broke down. A machine designed by a railway engineer and his son, weighing 4.3 tonnes and achieving a top speed of 48 km/h, won the £500 prize and the contract. It was the model for every subsequent steam locomotive.
events.revealBlurb: October 6-14, 1829 — George and Robert Stephenson's "Rocket" at Rainhill, between Liverpool and Manchester. Its multi-tube boiler was the design insight; earlier engines had used single large flues and wasted heat. The Rocket is preserved at London's Science Museum.

events.title: Bell Patents Telephone
events.blurb: A 29-year-old Scottish-born American inventor was granted a patent on "the method of, and apparatus for, transmitting vocal or other sounds telegraphically." Three days later he made the first recognized telephone call in his Boston laboratory, summoning his assistant from the next room. The patent, filed the same morning as a rival inventor's competing application, would become the most valuable patent ever issued by the US government.
events.revealBlurb: March 7, 1876 — Alexander Graham Bell. The first call: "Mr. Watson — come here — I want to see you." The rival, Elisha Gray, filed his caveat a few hours later; legal battles continued for years. American Telephone & Telegraph, founded on Bell's patent, became the largest corporation in the world.

events.title: Wright Brothers' First Flight
events.blurb: Two American bicycle-shop owners from Dayton, Ohio achieved the first sustained, controlled, powered flight of a heavier-than-air aircraft on a windswept dune at the Outer Banks of North Carolina. The first flight lasted 12 seconds and covered 36 metres — about the wingspan of a modern commercial airliner. They made three more flights that morning; the fourth covered 260 metres in 59 seconds. Few newspapers reported the achievement; commercial aviation took another three decades to arrive.
events.revealBlurb: December 17, 1903 — Orville and Wilbur Wright at Kill Devil Hills, near Kitty Hawk, NC. The flyer is now in the Smithsonian's National Air and Space Museum. The pair spent 4 years after their first flight battling patent disputes and litigation rather than manufacturing planes.

events.title: Altair 8800 Released
events.blurb: A cover article in an American hobbyist electronics magazine featured a $397 kit-build computer based on the Intel 8080 microprocessor, aimed at hardware enthusiasts willing to solder circuit boards and toggle binary instructions with front-panel switches. The magazine received over 2,000 kit orders in the first month. Among the Harvard students who saw the cover and wrote a BASIC interpreter for the machine were Bill Gates and Paul Allen.
events.revealBlurb: January 1975 — MITS Altair 8800, on the cover of Popular Electronics. Gates and Allen's BASIC would become the founding product of Microsoft. The Altair is universally credited as the first commercially successful microcomputer.

events.title: Microsoft Founded
events.blurb: A 19-year-old Harvard sophomore and his 22-year-old friend, working out of a cheap room in an Albuquerque motel, formally established a partnership to develop software for microcomputers. Their first product had been a BASIC interpreter for the Altair 8800, licensed to the kit's manufacturer. The contract paid royalties per machine sold. Within seven years they would own the personal-computer operating system industry.
events.revealBlurb: April 4, 1975 — Bill Gates and Paul Allen. Originally "Micro-Soft." They moved to the Seattle suburb of Bellevue in 1979 and to Redmond in 1986. Allen left the company in 1983 after being diagnosed with Hodgkin's lymphoma; he recovered, founded other businesses, died in 2018.

events.title: Apple II Released
events.blurb: A young Californian computer company released their second machine — and the first mass-market personal computer designed for non-hobbyists, with built-in color graphics, a working keyboard, a plastic case, and the ability to display text and graphics simultaneously. It shipped for $1,298 and found a broad market among small businesses, schools, and households. Apple's revenues grew 700 percent a year for five consecutive years.
events.revealBlurb: June 10, 1977 — Apple Computer. Engineered largely by Steve Wozniak. The arrival of VisiCalc two years later made it the first computer that small businesses felt they had to buy. Apple sold over 5 million Apple IIs before discontinuing the line in 1993.

events.title: iPhone Announced
events.blurb: A California computer company's co-founder unveiled a new class of mobile phone at a San Francisco conference, combining a widescreen iPod, a mobile internet browser, and a phone into a single slim device controlled entirely by a multi-touch finger-driven screen. He dialled a coffee shop on stage to demonstrate. Nokia's executives watching the announcement reportedly laughed at its lack of a physical keyboard; BlackBerry's CEO later admitted they also underestimated it.
events.revealBlurb: January 9, 2007 — Steve Jobs at Macworld. It went on sale June 29. The original did not support 3G, had no copy-and-paste, and shipped without an App Store — those all came in subsequent years. Apple now makes over $200 billion a year just from iPhones.

events.title: First Android Phone Released
events.blurb: A Taiwanese handset maker released the first commercial phone running an open-source mobile operating system developed by a Silicon Valley search-engine company, available through a US mobile carrier. The device had a physical keyboard that slid out from under the screen; unlike the rival iPhone, users could install apps from anywhere, replace the default apps, and generally modify the device at will. Open-ecosystem Android would grow to dominate global smartphone market share.
events.revealBlurb: October 22, 2008 — T-Mobile G1 (HTC Dream), running Android 1.0. Google had quietly acquired Android Inc. for $50 million in 2005. By 2013 more than half of smartphones sold ran Android; today it's over 70 percent globally.

events.title: Prabhat Film Company Founded
events.blurb: Five filmmakers and one jeweller-financier pooled ₹15,000 in a Kolhapur courtyard and established a studio whose name meant "Dawn" — it would go on to produce landmark Marathi and Hindi films through the 1930s, win the first Venice Film Festival prize awarded to an Asian film, and whose abandoned compound would later house the country's national film school.
events.revealBlurb: June 1, 1929 — founded by V. Shantaram and associates. Their 1936 film Sant Tukaram won a Venice award. When the studio folded in 1953, its Pune premises became the site of the Film and Television Institute of India.

events.title: Alam Ara Released — India's First Talkie
events.blurb: Police were deployed outside Majestic Cinema in Bombay that afternoon because the crowds gathering to hear a Hindi film speak for the first time overwhelmed the streets. The fantasy-romance had seven songs, making it arguably the first Bollywood musical; screenings sold out continuously for eight weeks, and the print of the film has since been completely lost.
events.revealBlurb: March 14, 1931 — directed by Ardeshir Irani. The film was shot in just 40 days. Every surviving account describes the audience's shock at hearing dialogue emerge from the screen, many reportedly weeping.

events.title: Kismet Released
events.blurb: A Bombay Talkies crime film with an unambiguous anti-hero — the lead character is a thief and a cad — opened in the depths of winter during a bitter internal dispute that was tearing the studio apart, yet became the first film in Indian cinema history to gross ₹1 crore. At a Calcutta cinema it ran for 187 consecutive weeks, a record that stood for 32 years.
events.revealBlurb: January 9, 1943, Bombay. Directed by Gyan Mukherjee, starring Ashok Kumar. Its patriotic song "Door Hato Ae Duniyawalon" — aimed at colonial occupation without naming it — spread through cities as independence agitation intensified. The British censors initially approved it without grasping the subtext.

events.title: Mughal-e-Azam Released
events.blurb: A Mughal-court epic that took sixteen years to complete — halted twice by financial collapse and partitioned away from its original cast — cost ₹1.5 crore, more than any previous Indian film, and spent ₹1 crore on a single song filmed in a replica of the Sheesh Mahal built with imported Belgian glass. Released in black and white, it was the highest-grossing Indian film for fifteen years.
events.revealBlurb: August 5, 1960 — directed by K. Asif. The original Akbar died before filming could restart; the entire cast was rebuilt after Partition. In 2004 it became the first Indian black-and-white film to be digitally colourised and theatrically re-released — and was a commercial success all over again.

events.title: Kaho Naa... Pyaar Hai Released
events.blurb: A double-role romantic thriller built around a completely unknown actor — son of its director — became the highest-grossing Hindi film of the year and won 92 awards across ceremonies, a figure the Guinness World Records certified as a record for any single film. The overnight stardom it generated was so total that magazine covers, television specials, and public hysteria followed within days.
events.revealBlurb: January 14, 2000 — directed by Rakesh Roshan, launching his son Hrithik. The film began production before Hrithik had done a single screen test beyond his father's living room. His dancing in the title track introduced a new male movement vocabulary to Bollywood that choreographers have referenced ever since.

events.title: The Indus Valley Cities Begin to Empty
events.blurb: Across a territory stretching from what is now Pakistan into Rajasthan, the carefully laid-out cities of the Indus civilization — Mohenjo-Daro, Harappa, Dholavira — began to be abandoned. Pottery quality declined, weights and measures lost standardization, and long-distance trade shrank. The most likely cause: a weakening of the summer monsoon and the drying of the Saraswati river system, which had sustained the civilization's agricultural surplus.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1900 BCE — beginning of Late Harappan period. The people did not vanish; they dispersed, many moving east toward the Gangetic plain. The ghost cities would not be rediscovered for 3,800 years, stumbled upon by a British railway surveyor in 1856.

events.title: Mahavira Attains Liberation
events.blurb: The 24th tirthankara of Jainism, who had wandered for 12 years in total asceticism — pulling out his hair by the roots, owning no possessions, eating only what was offered unsolicited — is believed by his followers to have shed his final karma and attained liberation at a town called Pavapuri in present-day Bihar. He died in a seated meditative posture, his body abandoned like a discarded garment.
events.revealBlurb: c. 527 BCE — Pavapuri, Bihar. Mahavira's teachings — ahimsa, satya, asteya, brahmacharya, aparigraha — became five of the most influential ethical concepts in Indian civilisation. Diwali, among Jains, commemorates his liberation.

events.title: Ashoka Conquers Kalinga
events.blurb: A Mauryan emperor's army conquered a fiercely resistant coastal kingdom after a war that, by the emperor's own inscriptions, killed 100,000 people and displaced 150,000 more. Revolted by the carnage he had ordered, the emperor publicly renounced war, embraced a philosophy of non-violence, and had pillars erected across his realm inscribed with edicts of compassion — the earliest dateable Indian texts we can read today.
events.revealBlurb: c. 261 BCE — Ashoka the Great, Maurya dynasty. The lion capital from his pillar at Sarnath — four lions standing back to back — is now India's national emblem.

events.title: Vasco da Gama Lands at Calicut
events.blurb: A Portuguese fleet rounded the tip of Africa and crossed the Indian Ocean, arriving at the most important spice port on the Malabar Coast. The Zamorin of Calicut received the visitors politely until he saw their gifts — cheap cloth and coral beads — and dismissed them. But the sea route was now open. Within decades, Portuguese cannon fire would dominate Indian Ocean trade routes that Arab, Persian, and Indian merchants had controlled for a thousand years.
events.revealBlurb: 20 May 1498 CE — Kozhikode (Calicut), Kerala. Da Gama's route around Africa was guided partly by an Indian navigator, Ahmad ibn Majid, who he reportedly bribed in Malindi. The pepper and spices he brought back to Lisbon were worth 60 times the voyage's cost.

events.title: The Marathas Are Defeated at the Third Battle of Panipat
events.blurb: A Maratha army of 45,000 soldiers and 200,000 camp followers — including families who had brought their children on what they expected to be a triumphant northern campaign — faced an Afghan force under the Durrani king. After an eight-month standoff that left the Marathas starving, they were crushed in a single morning. Between 60,000 and 70,000 troops died in the battle; up to 40,000 prisoners were massacred the following day.
events.revealBlurb: January 14, 1761 — Ahmad Shah Durrani vs. Sadashivrao Bhau, Panipat. Fought on the same plain as two earlier world-changing battles. The Maratha defeat ended Hindu imperial ambitions and opened India to British expansion. It is said that barely a family in the Deccan was not in mourning afterward.

events.title: Peloponnesian War Begins
events.blurb: Tensions between a democratic maritime empire led by Athens and an aristocratic land-based league led by Sparta erupted into open war when Spartan forces invaded Athenian-allied territory. The war would last 27 years, consume Greek wealth, shatter Athenian power, and undermine Greek confidence in the democratic project. A historian who had commanded an Athenian force early in the war produced a narrative account considered a founding masterpiece of Western historiography.
events.revealBlurb: 431 BCE — Athens vs. Sparta. The historian was Thucydides. A plague in 430 BCE killed perhaps a quarter of the Athenian population, including the city's leader Pericles. Athens finally surrendered in 404 BCE after its fleet was destroyed at Aegospotami; Socrates was executed in Athens five years later.

events.title: Silk Road Opens
events.blurb: A Chinese imperial envoy returning from a long mission into Central Asia reported the existence of advanced civilizations to the west. His court began dispatching trade missions through the oasis routes of Central Asia; within a century, Chinese silk was appearing in Roman markets, and Mediterranean glass was showing up in Han-dynasty tombs. The overland trade network — not a single road but a braided complex — would carry goods, people, religions, and epidemics across Eurasia for 1,500 years.
events.revealBlurb: c. 130 BCE — Zhang Qian's second mission, under Emperor Wu of Han. The term "Silk Road" was coined by 19th-century German geographer Ferdinand von Richthofen; no one in antiquity used the phrase. Buddhism reached China along it; the Black Death would as well.

events.title: Julius Caesar Assassinated
events.blurb: A Roman dictator, having been named dictator-for-life a month earlier, was stabbed 23 times by a group of 60 senators at a meeting of the Senate held in a Pompey-built theatre. The assassins, styling themselves "Liberators," had convinced themselves that removing the man who had effectively ended the Republic would restore it. Instead, his death plunged Rome into 14 more years of civil war, at the end of which his adopted heir emerged as the first Roman emperor in all but name.
events.revealBlurb: March 15, 44 BCE — the Ides of March. Conspirators included Brutus and Cassius. The supposed last words "Et tu, Brute?" come from Shakespeare; Caesar's actual last words — if he spoke any — may have been the Greek "kai su, teknon?" ("you too, my child?"). His heir Octavian defeated the conspirators at Philippi two years later.

events.title: Augustus Becomes Emperor
events.blurb: The Roman Senate formally voted a new series of titles and powers to the victor of the civil wars that had ended the Republic — including "Augustus" (the revered), "Princeps" (first citizen), and various senatorial and tribunicial powers. The Republic's forms were maintained — the Senate met, consuls were elected — but real power now flowed through the man at the top. The Roman Empire had begun. Its first emperor would reign 41 years and die of natural causes in his 75th year.
events.revealBlurb: January 16, 27 BCE — Octavian accepts the title "Augustus." He preferred the title "Princeps"; only later emperors would unambiguously style themselves "Imperator." The month August is named for him. He outlived his designated heirs repeatedly; his step-son Tiberius eventually succeeded him in 14 CE.

events.title: The Antonine Plague
events.blurb: Soldiers returning from campaigns in Parthia brought a disease — almost certainly smallpox — that spread from the eastern frontier through every province of the empire over fifteen years. The physician Galen, the most famous doctor of his age, documented symptoms in detail from Rome itself; at the plague's peak witnesses recorded 2,000 deaths per day in the capital alone.
events.revealBlurb: 165–180 CE. Galen's treatment recommendation included keeping patients warm and feeding them milk — the best care available, and completely ineffective. The plague killed co-emperor Lucius Verus in 169 CE and may have killed up to 10% of the empire's total population.

events.title: First Public Film Screening
events.blurb: Two French brothers, sons of a portrait photographer, held the first commercial screening of projected motion pictures in the basement of a Paris café. The audience of 33 paid one franc each to watch ten short films — workers leaving a factory, a baby being fed, a boat leaving a harbor. Their cinematograph was both camera and projector; the film was 35mm. Within a year their operators were touring every continent.
events.revealBlurb: December 28, 1895 — Louis and Auguste Lumière at the Salon Indien du Grand Café, Paris. The apocryphal story that audiences ran screaming from the train-arriving film comes from a later screening. The Lumières thought cinema was "an invention without a future" and quickly moved on to other projects.

events.title: Metropolis Released
events.blurb: A 36-year-old Austrian director released a 153-minute silent epic — at the time the most expensive film ever made — set in a stratified future city where wealthy elites enjoy skyscraper gardens above an underground inferno of machine-tending workers. The film's visual language — robot maidens, neon skylines, expressionist sets — shaped science-fiction imagery for the next century. The premiere had uneven reception; 40 minutes of footage were later cut.
events.revealBlurb: January 10, 1927 — Fritz Lang at the UFA-Palast am Zoo, Berlin. A reasonably complete version was pieced together only in 2008, when a 16mm print from the 1930s was found in a Buenos Aires archive. The robot Maria was voted the most important film robot in history.

events.title: Casablanca Premieres
events.blurb: A wartime romance set in a Moroccan cafe — produced on a tight schedule with an often-improvised script — premiered at a New York theater two weeks after Allied troops actually landed in the real-life city, a coincidence that boosted interest. The film's lead actor and actress had expected it to be a forgettable assignment; its dialogue's half-dozen phrases would be quoted by a century of audiences. Neither of the two stars was anyone's first choice for their parts.
events.revealBlurb: November 26, 1942 — Hollywood Theatre, NYC. Director Michael Curtiz, stars Humphrey Bogart and Ingrid Bergman. "Here's looking at you, kid" was Bogart's improvisation. "Play it again, Sam" is never actually said in the film.

events.title: Rashomon Released
events.blurb: A 40-year-old Japanese director released a 88-minute film in which the same violent encounter is recounted by four different participants, none of whom agrees with any of the others. The Venice Film Festival awarded it the Golden Lion the following year, and the world film industry discovered Japanese cinema as a major force. The very title became an English noun: "the Rashomon effect" is the concept of contradictory memories.
events.revealBlurb: August 26, 1950 — Akira Kurosawa. The producers were reportedly baffled by the script and wanted it re-edited. Its Venice win completely blindsided Japanese critics, who had not thought much of the film. It led directly to the global reception of Ozu, Mizoguchi, and Kurosawa's later work.

events.title: E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial Released
events.blurb: A 35-year-old American director released a 115-minute family film about a stranded alien befriended by a suburban boy who helps him contact his home planet. The director had developed the story as a way of processing his parents' divorce and his imaginary childhood companion. The film topped the box office for 16 weeks, displaced Star Wars as the highest-grossing film of all time, and moved children to tears for decades.
events.revealBlurb: June 11, 1982 — Steven Spielberg. Composer John Williams won the Oscar for his score; Spielberg himself didn't. The flying-bicycle silhouette against the moon became the logo of Amblin Entertainment, his production company.

events.title: Vasco da Gama Reaches India
events.blurb: A 29-year-old Portuguese captain, after a 10-month voyage south around the southern tip of Africa and up its eastern coast, dropped anchor at a spice port on the Malabar coast of India. He had sailed further than any previous European expedition. The local ruler was unimpressed by the trinkets he offered as tribute, but the sea route to Asian spices — breaking the Venetian and Arab overland monopoly — was now open.
events.revealBlurb: May 20, 1498 — Vasco da Gama at Calicut (Kozhikode), India. His expedition had left Lisbon with 170 men; 54 returned alive. He would make two more voyages and die in India in 1524 as the country's viceroy.

events.title: Cabral Reaches Brazil
events.blurb: A 33-year-old Portuguese nobleman commanding a 13-ship expedition bound for India — following Vasco da Gama's recent route — sailed so far west to catch favourable trade winds that he accidentally made landfall on a South American coast later named after a dyewood tree. He claimed it for Portugal under the six-year-old Tordesillas line and continued on to India. The accidental detour is the conventional starting point of Brazilian history.
events.revealBlurb: April 22, 1500 — Pedro Álvares Cabral in modern Bahia. He called the land "Ilha de Vera Cruz." Some historians think the "accidental" landfall was deliberate, responding to intelligence Portuguese mariners had gathered earlier. He lost six ships and over 100 men to storms en route onward to India.

events.title: Sistine Chapel Ceiling Unveiled
events.blurb: A 37-year-old Florentine sculptor, who had accepted a papal commission reluctantly after four years insisting he was not a painter, unveiled 500 square metres of freshly painted fresco covering the ceiling of a Vatican chapel. The work, which had taken four years, depicted nine scenes from Genesis surrounded by 300 figures. The artist had painted it while standing, not lying down as myth claims, his neck bent back for hours daily.
events.revealBlurb: October 31, 1512 — Michelangelo Buonarroti. He wrote a sonnet complaining of his neck: "I've grown a goiter by dwelling in this den… my beard turns up to heaven." Restoration between 1980 and 1994 revealed vivid colours under 400 years of candle smoke.

events.title: First Circumnavigation Complete
events.blurb: The last seaworthy ship of a Spanish expedition that had set out three years earlier with five vessels dropped anchor in the Guadalquivir River in Spain — the first ship ever to return to its port of departure after sailing completely around the world. Of the 270 men who had departed, 18 returned alive. Its captain, though no longer the expedition's original commander — who had been killed in the Philippines — had personally sailed the ship the entire way home.
events.revealBlurb: September 6, 1522 — Juan Sebastián Elcano aboard the Victoria. The voyage proved the earth was circumnavigable, and also forced the first adjustment of the ship's log by a day (a precursor to the concept of the International Date Line). Elcano himself died at sea in 1526, three ships into another expedition.

events.title: Galileo's Telescope Observations
events.blurb: A 46-year-old Paduan university mathematics professor, having improved the magnification of a newly invented Dutch optical toy from 3x to 30x, pointed his telescope at the night sky. Over the following months he observed craters on the moon, four previously unknown moons circling Jupiter, phases of Venus, and individual stars resolvable in the milky white band of the Milky Way. His findings, published in a short Latin book, transformed astronomy.
events.revealBlurb: January 7, 1610 — Galileo Galilei observed Jupiter's moons from Padua. His book "Sidereus Nuncius" (The Starry Messenger) was rushed into print in March. The phases of Venus, observed later that year, were decisive evidence against the Ptolemaic earth-centered model.

events.title: Wannsee Conference
events.blurb: Fifteen senior government and police officials gathered for a 90-minute meeting at a lakeside villa to coordinate the administrative, transportation, and security apparatus required to murder every Jewish person across an entire continent — a project already underway in the east that now needed to be extended westward in an organised and efficient manner.
events.revealBlurb: January 20, 1942, at a villa in the Berlin suburb of Wannsee. The meeting lasted 90 minutes and was followed by lunch. The Wannsee Protocol — the only surviving copy — was found after the war hidden in a filing cabinet. Not a single one of the 15 attendees objected to what was discussed.

events.title: Guadalcanal Landings
events.blurb: Marines waded ashore on a jungle island to seize a half-built airfield, kicking off a six-month campaign of grinding attrition across land, sea, and air that became the first major Allied offensive of the Pacific conflict. Both sides fed in reinforcements in a cycle of escalation while disease claimed more casualties than combat on either side.
events.revealBlurb: August 7, 1942 — the First Marine Division landed and took the airstrip without resistance. They renamed it Henderson Field after a Marine aviator killed at Midway. Over the next six months, at least 24 major naval engagements were fought in the surrounding waters, which sailors nicknamed "The Slot" and later "Ironbottom Sound."

events.title: Me 262's First All-Jet Flight
events.blurb: A swept-wing aircraft climbed away from a Bavarian airfield under pure jet power for the first time, reaching speeds that no piston-engined fighter could match, signalling that the era of propeller-driven military aviation was ending. The technology was real and available — but bureaucratic delays and a leadership obsession with bombers kept it from operational service for more than two years.
events.revealBlurb: July 18, 1942, Leipheim — pilot Fritz Wendel flew the Me 262 V3 on jet power alone for the first time. Hitler later insisted the aircraft be developed as a bomber rather than a fighter, reportedly costing Germany a 14-month delay. When it finally entered service in 1944, it was too little too late: fuel shortages kept most on the ground.

events.title: Rosie the Riveter Campaign
events.blurb: A deliberate government and industry campaign to recruit women into heavy industrial and weapons manufacturing work portrayed a bandana-wearing figure flexing her arm above the slogan "We Can Do It!" alongside magazine illustrations that reached millions of households, reshaping public expectations of gender and labour across a nation at industrial-scale mobilisation.
events.revealBlurb: 1942–1943. The number of women in the US workforce rose from 12 million to 20 million — a 57% increase — by 1944. Women built B-29s, welded Liberty ships, and operated cranes. The Westinghouse "We Can Do It!" poster was seen by almost no one during the war; it was rediscovered in the 1980s and became an icon of the feminist movement.

events.title: D-Day Landings
events.blurb: 156,000 Allied troops crossed the English Channel and landed on five code-named beaches along an 80-kilometre stretch of Normandy coast, supported by 11,000 aircraft sorties and 7,000 naval vessels. A massive deception operation convinced enemy commanders the real target was 300 kilometres further east.
events.revealBlurb: June 6, 1944 — Operation Overlord. Eisenhower carried a note in his pocket taking full blame if it failed. The "Mulberry" artificial harbours, towed across the Channel in pieces, unloaded two million tons of supplies in the months that followed. The first soldier ashore on Sword Beach was a British piper playing "Blue Bonnets Over the Border."

events.title: First Networked Email
events.blurb: A computer engineer working for a Cambridge, Massachusetts research firm sent an electronic message between two computers sitting next to each other in his office, using a symbol from the typewriter keyboard he'd picked precisely because it was never used in names — the "at" sign — to separate the user name from the host machine name. He could not recall years later what the message had contained; probably "QWERTYUIOP" or similar.
events.revealBlurb: October 1971 — Ray Tomlinson at BBN Technologies. The @ symbol's adoption was arbitrary but lasting. Tomlinson's contribution is the reason your email address contains an @. He died in 2016.

events.title: Wikipedia Launched
events.blurb: A 34-year-old internet entrepreneur who had been trying to build an online encyclopedia by paying credentialed experts to write and peer-review articles gave up on the slow model and switched to a radical alternative: a wiki, editable by anyone. The new version grew faster than expected. It had more articles in its first year than the slow-model version had produced in a previous eighteen months.
events.revealBlurb: January 15, 2001 — Jimmy Wales and Larry Sanger. By 2007 Wikipedia had surpassed Britannica in size and approximately in accuracy. Today's English Wikipedia has over 6.9 million articles, and the full project runs in 340+ languages.

events.title: Facebook Launched
events.blurb: A 19-year-old Harvard sophomore with a history of making unauthorized student-directory sites launched, from his dorm room, a social network restricted to students with harvard.edu email addresses. It reached half the Harvard student body within two weeks. He expanded to Yale, Columbia, and Stanford within weeks. Within a year he had dropped out; within four he was a billionaire on paper.
events.revealBlurb: February 4, 2004 — Mark Zuckerberg at Harvard, with co-founders Eduardo Saverin, Andrew McCollum, Dustin Moskovitz, and Chris Hughes. Originally thefacebook.com. Zuckerberg settled with the Winklevoss twins for $65 million in 2008; they spent it on Bitcoin.

events.title: Netflix Launches Streaming
events.blurb: A decade-old Silicon Valley mail-order DVD rental company launched an online video-streaming service, initially offering subscribers limited hours of instant streaming on top of their physical DVD subscriptions. The library at launch had about 1,000 titles and required Internet Explorer. The service would eventually make the DVD operation so irrelevant that the company's own name became an anachronism (net-flicks via mail).
events.revealBlurb: January 16, 2007 — initial subscribers got 1 hour of streaming per dollar paid per month. In 2011, CEO Reed Hastings attempted to split DVDs into a sister brand "Qwikster"; the backlash was so severe he reversed within three weeks.

events.title: WikiLeaks Cablegate
events.blurb: A whistleblower-platform website and a consortium of five newspapers began publishing, in coordinated waves, 251,287 U.S. diplomatic cables leaked by a 22-year-old U.S. Army intelligence analyst. The cables ranged from the mundane to the explosive — unflattering private assessments of world leaders, evidence of corruption in allied governments, and revelations about civilian deaths in Iraq and Afghanistan. The leaker would face the longest sentence ever imposed for leaking U.S. government information.
events.revealBlurb: November 28, 2010 — leaker Chelsea Manning (then Bradley), sentenced to 35 years in 2013. Obama commuted her sentence in 2017. WikiLeaks founder Julian Assange lived in the Ecuadorian embassy in London from 2012 until 2019; he was released from UK custody in a 2024 plea deal.

events.title: Chaucer's Canterbury Tales
events.blurb: An English civil servant in his mid-fifties died leaving unfinished a collection of stories told by pilgrims riding from Southwark to a Kentish cathedral shrine. Written in Middle English rather than French or Latin, the work demonstrated the poetic range of the English vernacular across a social spectrum — knights, millers, cooks, pardoners, the famously bawdy Wife of Bath. Only 24 of a planned 120 tales were ever completed.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1400 — Geoffrey Chaucer. He is often called the father of English literature. Roughly 80 manuscripts survive; the earliest complete ones date from the 1410s. The Wife of Bath's Tale became an early feminist touchstone.

events.title: Cervantes Publishes Don Quixote
events.blurb: A one-armed Spanish veteran, former galley slave, failed playwright, and occasional tax collector in his late fifties published a novel about a minor Spanish nobleman whose brain has been addled by reading too many romances and who rides out into rural Spain, helmet made from a barber's basin, to right imaginary wrongs. It sold out immediately; a pirated sequel appeared before he could write his own. His actual Part Two is often considered a greater achievement than Part One.
events.revealBlurb: January 1605 (Part 1), 1615 (Part 2) — Miguel de Cervantes. Part 2 contains the first known literary characters who know they are in a book — they have read Part 1. It is often called the first modern novel. Part 1 entered the public domain before Cervantes could profit much.

events.title: Treasure Island Published
events.blurb: A 33-year-old Scottish writer, suffering severe pulmonary illness and convalescing in the Scottish Highlands, sketched a treasure map with his 12-year-old stepson on a rainy afternoon and began improvising a story for the boy. The serialized pirate adventure novel that grew from the map — featuring a peg-legged cook, a squawking parrot, a buried fortune, and a black spot — essentially defined the iconography of piracy for the next century and a half.
events.revealBlurb: November 14, 1883 — Robert Louis Stevenson. Initially serialized in the magazine Young Folks in 1881 as "The Sea Cook." The phrase "Shiver me timbers!" does not appear in the book but was popularized by its Long John Silver.

events.title: Rabindranath Tagore Wins Nobel
events.blurb: A 52-year-old Bengali polymath — poet, novelist, philosopher, composer, painter — was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature, becoming the first non-European and the first Asian to receive the honour. The Swedish Academy specifically cited his English translation of his own Bengali poetry collection "Gitanjali." The award brought him international fame; at home in colonial India it cemented him as a national cultural figure.
events.revealBlurb: November 13, 1913 — Rabindranath Tagore. He renounced his British knighthood in 1919 after the Jallianwala Bagh Massacre. He composed the national anthems of both India ("Jana Gana Mana") and Bangladesh ("Amar Shonar Bangla"), two of three anthems he wrote for different countries.

events.title: 1984 Published
events.blurb: A 46-year-old English novelist, suffering from advanced tuberculosis on a remote Scottish island, published a dystopian novel depicting a totalitarian state where history is continuously rewritten, all speech is monitored, and a figurehead leader is omnipresent. He had been working on it for four years; he typed much of it lying in bed. He died of the disease seven months later. The book gave English a vocabulary for surveillance authoritarianism that has never been matched.
events.revealBlurb: June 8, 1949 — George Orwell (Eric Blair). Written on the island of Jura. "Big Brother," "doublethink," "thought police," "Newspeak," and "Orwellian" all entered English usage. The title's year was chosen by reversing 1948, the year he completed the draft.

events.title: Hammurabi Stele Carved
events.blurb: A Babylonian king had 282 laws carved onto a 2.25-metre-tall pillar of black basalt, topped with a relief showing him receiving his authority from the seated sun god Shamash. The laws range from compensation for surgical malpractice to rules on bride prices, with the refrain "if… then" throughout. The stele was carried off as war booty to Susa 600 years later and discovered there in 1901.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1754 BCE — Hammurabi, 6th king of the First Babylonian Dynasty. "An eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth" comes from here — law 196. Now in the Louvre. A second copy with slight variations was later found and is in Istanbul.

events.title: Tutankhamun Death Mask Created
events.blurb: Egyptian craftsmen fashioned a 10.2-kilogram gold funerary mask inlaid with lapis lazuli, carnelian, obsidian, and coloured glass to cover the mummy of a teenage pharaoh who had died at 18. The mask was sealed in a tomb packed with over 5,000 objects. The boy-king had been a minor figure; the tomb escaped the looting that emptied nearly every other Egyptian royal burial. It was untouched for 3,245 years.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1323 BCE — Tutankhamun died. Howard Carter's team uncovered the tomb on November 4, 1922. The mask now spends most of its time in a Cairo museum case and has been on world tours twice. The beard fell off during cleaning in 2014 and was hastily reattached with epoxy.

events.title: Raphael's School of Athens
events.blurb: A 28-year-old Umbrian painter completed the second of four monumental frescoes on the walls of the pope's private library at the Vatican, gathering the giants of classical philosophy into a single imaginary architectural space. Plato and Aristotle walk forward from a vanishing point; Pythagoras writes in a book, Euclid draws on a slate, Heraclitus leans alone on a block. The face of Euclid is the architect Bramante; Heraclitus is Michelangelo, working bitterly next door.
events.revealBlurb: 1511 — Raphael Sanzio, in the Stanza della Segnatura. The rivalry with Michelangelo, then painting the Sistine Ceiling a short walk away, was real; Raphael added him as an afterthought in a late revision.

events.title: Goya's Third of May 1808
events.blurb: A Spanish court painter in his late sixties completed a large canvas commemorating the execution of Spanish civilians by French occupying troops six years earlier. A man in a white shirt stretches his arms out cruciform, illuminated by a lantern at ground level; the executioners are faceless soldiers. The painting broke with the flattering conventions of history painting, depicting the victims as ordinary and terrified rather than heroic. Its brutality shocked its first audiences.
events.revealBlurb: 1814 — Francisco Goya. Commissioned, remarkably, by the restored Spanish monarch who the French had deposed — Ferdinand VII. Now in Madrid's Prado. It directly influenced Manet's Execution of Maximilian and Picasso's Guernica.

events.title: Munch's The Scream
events.blurb: A 30-year-old Norwegian painter completed the first version of a composition he had been sketching for years, showing a androgynous figure with an egg-shaped face and open mouth on a bridge above a blood-orange sky. The painter later wrote of the walk at dusk during which he had felt "a shriek passing through nature." He produced four versions across several decades; two have been stolen, and both were recovered.
events.revealBlurb: 1893 — Edvard Munch. The sky's colour may be real: it has been linked to the atmospheric effects of the Krakatoa eruption ten years earlier. The Oslo theft in 1994 happened during the opening ceremony of the Winter Olympics. The thieves left a note: "Thanks for the poor security."

events.title: Plessy v. Ferguson
events.blurb: The U.S. Supreme Court ruled 7-1 that a Louisiana law requiring "equal but separate" railroad cars for white and Black passengers did not violate the Constitution. The decision invented the "separate but equal" doctrine that underpinned legal segregation for 58 years. Justice John Marshall Harlan's lone dissent declared the Constitution "color-blind" — a minority view for half a century.
events.revealBlurb: May 18, 1896. The plaintiff, Homer Plessy, was 7/8 white; he deliberately boarded a whites-only car to test the law. Harlan, a former slaveholder from Kentucky, wrote the dissent the movement would eventually vindicate.

events.title: Little Rock Nine
events.blurb: Nine Black teenagers, escorted by federal troops, walked through the front doors of an Arkansas capital's previously all-white high school, three weeks after the governor had called out the National Guard to bar them. The images of the 101st Airborne at the schoolhouse door — bayonets fixed — broadcast on the nightly news forced a hostile public to confront massive resistance.
events.revealBlurb: September 25, 1957 — Central High School, Little Rock. President Eisenhower federalized the entire Arkansas National Guard to override Governor Orval Faubus. One of the nine, Elizabeth Eckford, was famously photographed walking alone through a screaming mob on an earlier attempt.

events.title: Birmingham Children's Crusade
events.blurb: Over several days in a notoriously segregated Alabama steel city, more than a thousand Black schoolchildren — some as young as 6 — marched out of classes in organized protest. Police commissioner Bull Connor ordered fire hoses and attack dogs deployed against them. Photographs of a teenage boy lunged at by a German shepherd appeared on front pages across the world.
events.revealBlurb: May 2-5, 1963 — Birmingham, Alabama. King agreed to use children over the objections of many advisers; they were less vulnerable to losing jobs for protesting. Within weeks, the Kennedy administration introduced what became the Civil Rights Act.

events.title: Shirley Chisholm's Presidential Run
events.blurb: A Brooklyn congresswoman, four years after becoming the first Black woman elected to the U.S. Congress, announced her candidacy for the presidency. She was the first African-American to seek a major party's nomination and the first woman to seek the Democratic one. Her slogan was "Unbought and Unbossed." She earned 152 convention delegates before Senator George McGovern won the nomination.
events.revealBlurb: January 25, 1972. She had to sue to be included in televised debates. She survived three assassination attempts during the campaign. "When I ran," she said later, "I ran because someone had to do it first."

events.title: George Floyd Murdered
events.blurb: A 46-year-old Black man was killed in a Midwestern American city when a white police officer kneeled on his neck for 9 minutes and 29 seconds while he was handcuffed face-down on the pavement. A 17-year-old bystander filmed the entire encounter on her phone. The video triggered the largest protest movement in American history — 15 to 26 million people marched across all 50 states over the following weeks.
events.revealBlurb: May 25, 2020 — Minneapolis, officer Derek Chauvin. The bystander was Darnella Frazier; she received a Pulitzer Prize special citation. Chauvin was convicted of second-degree murder 11 months later and sentenced to 22 years. Protests spread to more than 60 countries.

events.title: Pac-Man Reaches North America
events.blurb: A Japanese arcade cabinet featuring a yellow circular character navigating a maze while consuming dots and evading four coloured ghosts began distribution across North American arcades. Within 18 months it had been installed in over 100,000 locations and grossed more revenue than all theatrical box office receipts in America that year combined.

events.title: CNN Launches
events.blurb: A 24-hour cable news network began broadcasting from a converted country-club headquarters in a southeastern U.S. city, defying widespread industry skepticism that there was enough daily news to fill a full day of programming. The network's first broadcast began with its founder and his wife standing in front of an American flag. Its approach — continuous live coverage, rolling updates, no fixed broadcast schedule — eventually reshaped how all news was delivered.
events.revealBlurb: June 1, 1980 — Ted Turner's Cable News Network, Atlanta. The Gulf War coverage in 1991, broadcast live from Baghdad as bombs fell, established CNN's dominance. Turner had filmed a doomsday video, intended to play only at the literal end of the world, saying farewell to viewers.

events.title: Thriller Album Released
events.blurb: A recording artist released a 42-minute album featuring nine tracks, seven of which became top-ten singles on the Billboard Hot 100 — a chart achievement never matched before or since. The album sold more than 66 million copies, and its 14-minute title-track music video transformed the medium from a promotional clip into an art form.

events.title: Apple's "1984" Super Bowl Ad
events.blurb: A 60-second commercial produced by a British director for a California computer company aired during the third quarter of the Super Bowl. The ad showed a dystopian audience of grey workers watching a Big-Brother-like speaker on a vast screen; an athletic woman in running clothes smashed the screen with a hammer. The product was the Macintosh computer. Apple's board had voted to kill the ad; the CEO insisted it air. It aired once.
events.revealBlurb: January 22, 1984 — directed by Ridley Scott. The ad ran nationally only that one time; it has since been shown as a promotion or film-clip thousands of times. Macintosh sales in its first 100 days exceeded expectations. The "1984" ad is still considered one of the greatest commercials ever made.

events.title: Seinfeld Premieres
events.blurb: A 90-minute pilot episode titled "The Seinfeld Chronicles" aired on NBC, starring a 35-year-old New York stand-up comedian as a fictionalized version of himself and three friends navigating petty social minutiae in Manhattan. NBC had almost dropped the show; test audiences had responded coolly. A show famously about "nothing," it would run 180 episodes over nine seasons and become one of the most influential sitcoms in television history.
events.revealBlurb: July 5, 1989 — Jerry Seinfeld, Jason Alexander, Michael Richards (Julia Louis-Dreyfus joined season 2). Co-creator Larry David later made Curb Your Enthusiasm, essentially a Seinfeld-universe spinoff. The cast famously turned down $5 million per episode each to continue past season 9.

events.title: Susan B. Anthony Votes
events.blurb: A 52-year-old suffragist and 14 other women presented themselves at a polling place in their upstate New York city and demanded to register to vote, citing the language of the recently ratified 14th Amendment. Three inspectors, after consulting the U.S. constitution, let them register. On election day four days later she voted; she was arrested two weeks after that. Her trial, the following year, denied her the right to testify in her own defense.
events.revealBlurb: November 5, 1872 — Rochester, NY. Judge Ward Hunt fined her $100; she refused ever to pay. The U.S. has since put her face on a coin that was widely disliked and quickly withdrawn (the 1979 dollar).

events.title: First Woman Prime Minister
events.blurb: The widow of an assassinated South Asian island-nation prime minister was sworn in as his successor, becoming the first woman to lead a national government anywhere in the world. She had entered politics only after her husband's murder the previous year. She would serve three separate terms over four decades, dying in office at age 84.
events.revealBlurb: July 21, 1960 — Sirimavo Bandaranaike of Ceylon (now Sri Lanka). She led a non-aligned left-of-center government; her daughter Chandrika became president 34 years later. She died on November 13, 2000, after casting her vote in a general election.

events.title: FDA Approves the Pill
events.blurb: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved a daily oral contraceptive pill combining synthetic estrogen and progestin for sale as a birth-control product, two years after approving the same drug for menstrual disorders. Over two million American women were taking it within three years. It was the first drug ever developed for use by healthy people rather than sick ones, and it reshaped women's labour-force participation for the next half-century.
events.revealBlurb: May 9, 1960 — Enovid, made by G.D. Searle. The research had been funded privately by heiress Katharine McCormick because federal funding was politically impossible. Single women could be denied prescriptions until a 1972 Supreme Court ruling.

events.title: Roe v. Wade
events.blurb: The U.S. Supreme Court ruled 7-2 that the right to privacy implicit in the 14th Amendment protected a woman's decision to terminate a pregnancy, striking down most state abortion laws. The ruling established a three-trimester framework balancing state interests against individual rights. It would remain the governing precedent for 49 years, until its overturn in 2022 returned abortion regulation to the states.
events.revealBlurb: January 22, 1973 — plaintiff "Jane Roe" was Norma McCorvey, who never actually had the abortion. She changed her position on the issue multiple times before her death in 2017. The ruling was overturned by Dobbs v. Jackson on June 24, 2022.

events.title: Kamala Harris Becomes VP
events.blurb: A 56-year-old U.S. senator from California, whose mother had immigrated from India and father from Jamaica, was sworn in on the steps of the U.S. Capitol as the nation's 49th vice president, the first woman, first African-American, and first Asian-American to hold the office. She was sworn in by the first Latina Supreme Court justice, on two bibles: one from Justice Thurgood Marshall's widow and one from a close family friend.
events.revealBlurb: January 20, 2021 — sworn in by Justice Sonia Sotomayor. The inauguration, held two weeks after the January 6 Capitol attack, proceeded behind 25,000 National Guard troops. Harris later became the 2024 Democratic presidential nominee after Joe Biden withdrew.

events.title: Eruption of Vesuvius
events.blurb: A volcano on the Italian peninsula, dormant for centuries and believed extinct by the farmers whose vineyards clung to its slopes, erupted in a single day, burying two wealthy resort towns and their roughly 16,000 inhabitants under 6 metres of ash, pumice, and pyroclastic flow. The buried cities lay undiscovered for 1,700 years.
events.revealBlurb: August 24, 79 CE — Pompeii and Herculaneum, under Mount Vesuvius. Pliny the Younger watched from across the Bay of Naples and wrote the only eyewitness account. Volcanologists still classify massive plinian eruptions by his name.

events.title: Shaanxi Earthquake
events.blurb: The deadliest earthquake in recorded human history struck a densely populated region of northern China in the early morning, collapsing hillsides dotted with cave dwellings carved from soft loess soil. Roughly 830,000 people died — some 60 percent of the population of the affected counties. In some districts, everyone was killed.
events.revealBlurb: January 23, 1556 — Shaanxi Province, Ming Dynasty. The loess hillsides, prized for their insulation, became mass graves when the quake liquefied them. The toll remains a single-event record four and a half centuries later.

events.title: Krakatoa Eruption
events.blurb: An island volcano in the strait between two large Indonesian islands exploded in a series of detonations culminating in a final blast so loud it was heard 4,800 kilometres away and circled the planet four times as a pressure wave. The eruption generated tsunamis that killed 36,000 people on surrounding coasts; the resulting atmospheric dust produced red-green sunsets worldwide for years.
events.revealBlurb: August 27, 1883 — Krakatoa, Sunda Strait. The final explosion had an acoustic energy roughly equivalent to 200 megatons of TNT. The glow of the afterburn may be what Edvard Munch painted in The Scream a decade later.

events.title: Mount St. Helens Eruption
events.blurb: A Pacific Northwest volcano that had been swelling a grotesque 150-metre bulge on its north flank for two months underwent a catastrophic lateral blast triggered by an earthquake. The collapse produced the largest landslide in recorded history, flattening 600 square kilometres of forest and killing 57 people, including a stubborn innkeeper who refused to evacuate.
events.revealBlurb: May 18, 1980 — Washington State, USA. The innkeeper was Harry R. Truman, 83, who kept pets and a collection of bourbon at his lodge and became a folk hero for his refusal to leave. His body was never found.

events.title: Kobe Earthquake
events.blurb: A magnitude 6.9 earthquake struck a major Japanese port city in the early morning, collapsing expressway sections and igniting fires that destroyed some 7,000 wooden houses. 6,434 people died. The initial government response was famously sluggish — organized yakuza crime syndicates distributed relief supplies before the army arrived.
events.revealBlurb: January 17, 1995 — Kobe. The elevated Hanshin Expressway fell sideways onto its support pillars, a widely published image of post-war Japanese infrastructure failure. The Aum Shinrikyo cult's Tokyo subway sarin attack followed two months later, making 1995 a traumatic year for Japan.

events.title: Explorer 1 — First US Satellite
events.blurb: A Juno I rocket launched the United States' first satellite from Cape Canaveral, placing an 8.3 kg cylinder into an elliptical orbit that reached 2,550 km altitude. The satellite's Geiger–Müller tube detected a region of intense radiation surrounding Earth — data that led James Van Allen to identify the radiation belts bearing his name.
events.revealBlurb: January 31, 1958 — Explorer 1. The US had been beaten to orbit by Sputnik 1 and Sputnik 2 in the previous three months. In a press conference photo, three scientists hoisted a full-scale model over their heads in triumph — the actual satellite weighed less than a toaster oven. Explorer 1 remained in orbit for 12 years.

events.title: First American in Space
events.blurb: Alan Shepard rode a Redstone rocket on a 15-minute suborbital arc reaching 187 km altitude, becoming the first American in space — 23 days after Yuri Gagarin's orbital flight. Unlike Gagarin's automated mission, Shepard manually controlled his capsule's attitude during the flight using a hand controller, though the arc itself was ballistic and unpowered.
