events.revealBlurb: May 5, 1961 — Freedom 7. Shepard had been suited up and waiting in the capsule for four hours through repeated launch delays. At one point he radioed mission control: "Why don't you fix your little problem and light this candle?" His answer came 15 minutes later. He was weightless for only 5 minutes of the flight.

events.title: First Woman in Space
events.blurb: Valentina Tereshkova, a 26-year-old former textile factory worker and amateur parachutist with no pilot training, launched aboard Vostok 6 and orbited Earth 48 times over nearly three days — more total time in space than all US astronauts who had flown to that date combined. She performed observations and photographed aerosol layers in Earth's atmosphere before parachuting to a landing in Kazakhstan.
events.revealBlurb: June 16, 1963 — Vostok 6. Tereshkova selected herself from 400 applicants by writing a letter directly to the Soviet Space Program. She reportedly got motion sick and did not conduct some planned manual maneuvers, a fact kept classified for years. No woman flew in space again for 19 years. She remains the only woman to have flown a solo space mission.

events.title: Challenger Disintegration
events.blurb: Space Shuttle Challenger broke apart 73 seconds after launch when a rubber O-ring seal on the right solid rocket booster failed in overnight temperatures that had dropped to -8 °C, allowing combustion gases to breach the joint and sever the external tank. All seven crew members were killed, including Christa McAuliffe, who had been selected from more than 11,000 applicants for NASA's Teacher in Space program.
events.revealBlurb: January 28, 1986 — STS-51-L. Engineers at Morton Thiokol had urged a launch delay the night before, citing O-ring behavior in cold temperatures; NASA managers overruled them. The crew cabin survived the initial breakup intact and fell for nearly three minutes before striking the Atlantic at roughly 320 km/h.

events.title: First Orbital Rocket Booster Landing
events.blurb: A SpaceX Falcon 9 first stage returned from an orbital-class mission and landed upright at Landing Zone 1 in Cape Canaveral, completing the first successful recovery of an orbital-class rocket booster under propulsive control. The same vehicle had delivered 11 commercial satellites to orbit minutes earlier and touched down within about 10 meters of the target pad.
events.revealBlurb: December 21, 2015 — OG-2 Mission 2. SpaceX had attempted and failed four previous booster landings on a drone ship at sea. The Falcon's legs deployed at 180 m altitude. Elon Musk posted one word after confirmation: "Welcome back, baby." The reused booster concept cut launch costs by roughly 30%.

events.title: Gandhi Assassinated
events.blurb: A 78-year-old man, walking slowly across a Delhi lawn supported by two of his grandnieces, was shot three times in the chest at point-blank range by a Hindu nationalist who blamed him for indulging Muslims and accepting partition. He fell murmuring the name of a god. He had survived five previous attempts on his life.
events.revealBlurb: January 30, 1948 — the assassin was Nathuram Godse, a former editor of a Hindu nationalist newspaper. He was convicted and executed. Gandhi had warned his secretary that morning that his life's work would not be judged "until after I am dead and gone."

events.title: Constitution of India Adopted
events.blurb: A constituent assembly of 299 members, chaired by a Bombay-trained lawyer from a once-"untouchable" community, completed two years and eleven months of debate to enact the longest written national constitution in the world — 395 articles, 22 parts, 8 schedules — establishing a secular, socialist, democratic republic. It came into force on the anniversary of a 1930 declaration of complete independence.
events.revealBlurb: January 26, 1950 — B.R. Ambedkar, chair of the drafting committee. The date — Republic Day — was chosen because it marked the 20th anniversary of Congress's Purna Swaraj declaration. The final handwritten copy is illuminated by the artist Nandalal Bose.

events.title: Indo-Pakistani War of 1965
events.blurb: Infiltrators crossed the ceasefire line into a disputed northern territory to incite a rebellion that failed to materialize. India retaliated by invading across the international border toward a major Pakistani city. Seventeen days of conventional ground and air combat across the Punjab plains ended in stalemate, with each side convinced it had won. 3,000 Indian and 3,800 Pakistani soldiers died.
events.revealBlurb: August-September 1965 — ended by the Tashkent Declaration in January. The Battle of Asal Uttar saw one of the largest tank battles since WWII. Neither side's territorial changes amounted to much, and what they gained was returned at Tashkent.

events.title: Bangladesh Liberation War
events.blurb: Pakistan's army launched a crackdown on the Bengali-speaking eastern wing of its own country, displacing an estimated 10 million refugees across the border into India. India intervened militarily; within thirteen days it had driven the Pakistani army to capitulate in a Bengali capital, where 93,000 surrendered in the largest military surrender since WWII. A new nation was born.
events.revealBlurb: December 3-16, 1971 — victory at the Instrument of Surrender at Ramna Race Course, Dhaka. Bangladesh Liberation Day is December 16. Field Marshal Sam Manekshaw commanded the Indian effort; Lt. General A.A.K. Niazi signed the surrender.

events.title: Pokhran-II Nuclear Tests
events.blurb: India conducted five underground nuclear explosions over two days in the same Rajasthani desert test range it had used 24 years earlier, including a claimed thermonuclear device. The tests, carried out in conditions of extraordinary operational security that surprised American intelligence satellites, declared the country a full nuclear-weapon state. Pakistan tested its own devices 17 days later.
events.revealBlurb: May 11 and 13, 1998 — code-named Operation Shakti. Prime Minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee had been in office three months. Sanctions were imposed; they were lifted within two years as the United States reassessed its South Asia policy.

events.title: Sony Walkman Released
events.blurb: A Japanese electronics company released a portable personal cassette player, weighing 390 grams, with headphones instead of a speaker. It had no record function — unusual for a cassette player — and its CEO personally insisted on this as a way of encouraging private, solitary music consumption. The device created an entirely new product category and pulled portable listening out of the car radio and boombox and into the individual's pocket for the next quarter-century.
events.revealBlurb: July 1, 1979 — Sony TPS-L2. Co-founder Masaru Ibuka had wanted something compact to enjoy opera on long flights. The original name in Japan was "Walkman"; in the US, "Soundabout"; in the UK, "Stowaway." "Walkman" eventually won out globally.

events.title: Macintosh Launched
events.blurb: A California computer company launched a new desktop computer during a Super Bowl advertising spot, and formally introduced it at a shareholders meeting two days later. The machine had a 9-inch black-and-white screen, a mouse, a graphical user interface with icons and windows, and pull-down menus — none of which had previously shipped on a mass-market computer. It cost $2,495 and would struggle commercially against the cheaper IBM PC for years.
events.revealBlurb: January 24, 1984 — Apple Macintosh. Ridley Scott's "1984" Super Bowl ad ran on January 22. The original Mac shipped with 128KB of memory; Bill Gates had quietly promised Steve Jobs a version of MS Word for it.

events.title: Google Founded
events.blurb: Two Stanford doctoral students incorporated a search engine company whose name derived from the mathematical term for 10 to the power of 100. Their PageRank algorithm ranked results by treating hyperlinks as votes, producing more relevant results than the keyword-frequency systems that dominated at the time.

events.title: iMac Released
events.blurb: A California computer company, newly returned to profitability under a recently returned co-founder, released an all-in-one desktop machine housed in a translucent Bondi-blue plastic case, with no floppy drive, a built-in USB port, and a round puck of a mouse. Industrial designer Jonathan Ive had led the design. The machine was derided on spec by some industry press; it sold over 800,000 units in the first five months and rescued the company's consumer business.
events.revealBlurb: August 15, 1998 — Apple iMac G3, designed by Jonathan Ive under Steve Jobs. The "i" prefix, coined by copywriter Ken Segall, would carry over to iPod, iPhone, iPad, iCloud. The translucent plastic shell was revolutionary for its time.

events.title: BlackBerry Released
events.blurb: A Canadian wireless technology company released a two-way pager with a small keyboard and a monochrome screen that could also receive email. Corporate IT departments loved it — executives could finally stay in touch while traveling — and within a few years the device had become a status symbol and, later, an addiction. Users typed with thumbs on the tiny QWERTY keys; the resulting repetitive-strain injury acquired the nickname "BlackBerry thumb."
events.revealBlurb: January 19, 1999 — Research In Motion's BlackBerry 850. Chosen name because the keyboard's buttons resembled the drupelets of a blackberry fruit. The iPhone's 2007 arrival began BlackBerry's long decline; RIM pivoted to BlackBerry Ltd. and left hardware in 2016.

events.title: Deposition of Romulus Augustulus
events.blurb: The Germanic warlord Odoacer deposed the sixteen-year-old emperor Romulus Augustulus at Ravenna — a boy whose mocking nickname meant "Little Augustus" — and sent the imperial regalia to Constantinople, informing the eastern emperor that the west no longer needed a separate ruler. Odoacer spared Romulus's life, finding him too young and too minor to bother executing, and exiled him to a villa in Campania on a pension.
events.revealBlurb: September 4, 476 CE. The last western emperor's name combined the city's legendary founder and its first emperor — an irony Roman writers noticed immediately. Contemporaries did not regard this moment as "the fall of Rome"; that framing came centuries later. The eastern empire in Constantinople continued for another 977 years.

events.title: The Hijra
events.blurb: Fleeing plots against his life in the Arabian trading city where he had preached for 13 years, a 53-year-old prophet and roughly seventy of his followers slipped out at night and rode 320 kilometres north to a rival oasis town whose feuding tribes had invited him to mediate. He arrived to a welcoming reception and began building the first Islamic community under his political authority.
events.revealBlurb: July 16, 622 — Muhammad's migration from Mecca to Medina. The Islamic calendar begins from this year, not his birth. "Hijra" literally means "emigration" or "severing of ties."

events.title: Walk to Canossa
events.blurb: A Holy Roman Emperor, excommunicated by the pope over who had the right to appoint bishops, traveled across the Alps in the dead of winter and stood barefoot in a hair shirt in the snow outside a mountain fortress in northern Italy for three days, begging absolution. The pope eventually let him in and lifted the excommunication. The image of imperial submission to papal authority would haunt European politics for centuries.
events.revealBlurb: January 25-28, 1077 — Henry IV before Pope Gregory VII at Canossa. "To go to Canossa" became a European idiom for humiliating capitulation. Henry later recovered his throne, marched on Rome, and installed his own antipope, so the humbling was strategic rather than spiritual.

events.title: Marco Polo Departs for China
events.blurb: A 17-year-old Venetian merchant's son set out with his father and uncle on a journey across Asia to the court of the Mongol emperor. He would return to Venice 24 years later and, captured in a war with Genoa three years after that, dictate an account of his travels to a cellmate. The resulting book became the most influential western description of Asia for the next three centuries.
events.revealBlurb: 1271 — Marco left Venice with Niccolò and Maffeo Polo. Returning in 1295, he was imprisoned by the Genoese; his cellmate Rustichello da Pisa helped him write "Il Milione." Christopher Columbus's annotated copy survives.

events.title: Fall of Granada
events.blurb: The last Muslim ruler of an Andalusian emirate, besieged for seven months in his Alhambra palace, handed over its keys to Castilian and Aragonese monarchs and rode into exile, reportedly sighing at his final view from a mountain pass. The surrender ended 781 years of Muslim political presence on the Iberian peninsula. The same monarchs, three months later, would commission an Italian sailor to seek a western route to Asia.
events.revealBlurb: January 2, 1492 — Ferdinand and Isabella accept the surrender of Muhammad XII (Boabdil). His mother is said to have told him: "You weep like a woman for what you could not defend like a man." Columbus was at the Alhambra that summer presenting his proposal.

events.title: FIFA Founded
events.blurb: Representatives of seven European national football associations — Belgium, Denmark, France, Netherlands, Spain, Sweden, and Switzerland — met at a Paris sports association's offices and established an international governing body for the sport. England, which had invented the modern codified game and considered itself the natural authority, declined to attend, joined in 1905, and withdrew multiple times over subsequent decades in petty disputes. The organization would run the World Cup from 1930 on.
events.revealBlurb: May 21, 1904 — Fédération Internationale de Football Association, Paris. Its first president was Robert Guérin. FIFA now has 211 member associations, more than the UN. Its headquarters moved to Zurich in 1932 and have been there since.

events.title: Battle of the Sexes Tennis Match
events.blurb: A 29-year-old professional tennis player defeated a 55-year-old former Wimbledon champion in straight sets before a crowd of 30,000 at the Houston Astrodome and a television audience of 90 million. The retired player had publicly declared that no woman could defeat him, offering a $100,000 prize to any who tried.

events.title: Tiger Woods Wins First Masters
events.blurb: A 21-year-old American golfer, playing in his first Masters as a professional, won the prestigious Augusta tournament by 12 strokes — the largest margin in the event's history — with a record-setting 18-under-par total. He was the youngest winner of a Masters, the first with African ancestry, and the first of Asian heritage. The club had admitted its first Black member only seven years earlier. Viewership had doubled the previous year's; his arrival reshaped the demographics, marketing, and money of professional golf.
events.revealBlurb: April 13, 1997 — Tiger Woods at Augusta National. He would win 15 major championships across a career including three more Masters wins. His dominance of the sport from 1997 through 2008 has been widely called one of the most influential individual runs in professional sports.

events.title: Cubs Win World Series
events.blurb: The Chicago Cubs won their first World Series championship in 108 years, defeating the Cleveland Indians in a 10-inning seventh game interrupted by a rain delay. The Cubs' championship drought — dating back to 1908 — was the longest in American professional sports. Their 1945 loss had been attributed by fans to the "Curse of the Billy Goat," thrown at the owner of a neighbourhood tavern who had been asked to remove his pet goat from a World Series game.
events.revealBlurb: November 2-3, 2016 — Cubs 8, Indians 7 in 10 innings at Progressive Field, Cleveland. The game ended at 12:47 AM local time on November 3. Cubs manager Joe Maddon, third baseman Kris Bryant, and first baseman Anthony Rizzo led the championship team. Chicago celebrated with a victory parade of 5 million people.

events.title: Kobe Bryant Dies
events.blurb: A 41-year-old retired basketball star, his 13-year-old daughter, and seven other passengers died when their private helicopter crashed into a hillside in thick fog outside Los Angeles while en route to a youth basketball game. The retired player had won five NBA championships, two Olympic golds, and the nickname "Black Mamba" during a 20-year career entirely with the Los Angeles Lakers. The crash prompted an outpouring of mourning around the world.
events.revealBlurb: January 26, 2020 — Kobe and Gianna Bryant. National Transportation Safety Board findings attributed the crash to pilot error in poor visibility. His 2017 jersey-retirement ceremony at Staples Center saw both his numbers (8 and 24) raised to the rafters — the only player in franchise history with multiple retired numbers.

events.title: Battle of the Coral Sea
events.blurb: Two opposing fleets manoeuvred for days without either side's surface ships ever sighting the other, their aircraft flying hundreds of miles over open ocean to find and strike carriers whose decks they could not see. One navy lost a fleet carrier and the other lost a light carrier — but the strategic consequence was that an invasion convoy turned back.
events.revealBlurb: May 4–8, 1942 — the first naval battle in history fought entirely by aircraft. Neither fleet's ships came within sight of the other. Japan lost the light carrier Shōhō; the US lost USS Lexington. The two Japanese fleet carriers damaged at Coral Sea were then unavailable at Midway — a fact that proved decisive a month later.

events.title: V-2 Rocket's First Successful Test
events.blurb: A 14-metre liquid-fuelled rocket rose from a Baltic coast test site, climbed above the atmosphere, and travelled 190 kilometres before splashing down — the first object built by human hands to reach space, demonstrating a weapon that could strike cities at supersonic speed with no interception possible by any existing technology.
events.revealBlurb: October 3, 1942, Peenemünde. General Walter Dornberger declared: "This third day of October is the first day of a new era, that of space travel." The same technology later launched the first satellites and moon rockets. The V-2's wartime manufacture killed more people in slave-labour production than it killed as a weapon.

events.title: Battle of Stalingrad
events.blurb: For six months, a city named after a living leader was fought over house by house, factory floor by factory floor, in temperatures reaching minus 40 degrees, as an encircled attacking force slowly starved and froze while its commander received a field marshal's baton and an order never to surrender. The first capitulation of an entire German field army in the war followed 12 days later.
events.revealBlurb: August 1942 – February 2, 1943. Of the 330,000 who entered the Stalingrad pocket, 91,000 surrendered — including 24 generals and Field Marshal Friedrich Paulus. Fewer than 6,000 of those prisoners ever returned to Germany. Hitler promoted Paulus to Field Marshal the day before surrender, noting no German field marshal had ever been taken alive.

events.title: Italy's Armistice Announcement
events.blurb: A radio broadcast by a head of government announced that his country had signed an armistice with the opposing alliance, pulling out of an axis it had helped found, leaving its former partner's forces — which had already occupied key positions across the country — to decide how to respond. German forces immediately disarmed Italian troops and occupied cities across the peninsula.
events.revealBlurb: September 8, 1943 — Marshal Badoglio's broadcast at 7:42 PM. The armistice had actually been signed on September 3 but was kept secret. German Operation Achse activated within hours, disarming and capturing roughly 650,000 Italian soldiers. Many were sent to German labour camps; some 50,000 died in captivity. The king and Badoglio fled Rome before dawn.

events.title: Liberation of Auschwitz
events.blurb: Soviet soldiers opened the gates of a vast camp complex to find several thousand survivors too ill to have been force-marched away, alongside 1.2 million items of women's clothing, 43,000 pairs of shoes, seven tonnes of human hair, and industrial quantities of Zyklon B — physical evidence of the systematic murder of more than a million people.
events.revealBlurb: January 27, 1945. The 60th Army of the 1st Ukrainian Front liberated roughly 7,000 remaining prisoners. The SS had dynamited the crematoria weeks earlier to destroy evidence. January 27 is now the United Nations' International Holocaust Remembrance Day. The surviving Sonderkommando testimonies buried in the ash confirmed what the physical evidence already showed.

events.title: Plato's Republic
events.blurb: An Athenian philosopher completed a ten-book Socratic dialogue in which his deceased teacher argues with several interlocutors about the nature of justice and, by extension, the ideal city. The work would become the foundational text of Western political philosophy; its allegory of the cave, its philosopher-king proposal, and its ban on poets have been quoted, contested, and imitated ever since.
events.revealBlurb: c. 380 BCE — Plato. Alfred North Whitehead famously called European philosophy "a series of footnotes to Plato." The Republic was unknown in the medieval Latin West until the Renaissance; it reached Islamic and Byzantine scholars first.

events.title: Gutenberg Bible Printed
events.blurb: A goldsmith in a Rhine-valley city completed the first book printed in Europe using movable metal type — a Latin Bible set in 42 lines per page, bound in 180 copies. His press combined existing technologies — oil-based ink, a wine-press frame, cast-metal punches — into an invention that would be blamed for everything from the Reformation to the Renaissance to modern literacy.
events.revealBlurb: 1455 — Johannes Gutenberg in Mainz. Forty-nine copies are known to survive; roughly twenty are complete. Gutenberg himself was sued by his financier the same year and lost the press.

events.title: Johnson's Dictionary Published
events.blurb: An Oxford-educated English essayist, working nine years with six assistants in a garret flat, completed and published a two-volume dictionary of the English language — the first comprehensive, systematically illustrated dictionary of the vernacular. It defined 42,773 words with 114,000 quotations showing their use. It was the standard English dictionary until Oxford's larger project finally superseded it 173 years later.
events.revealBlurb: April 15, 1755 — Samuel Johnson. He defined "lexicographer" as "a harmless drudge, that busies himself in tracing the original, and detailing the signification of words." His tart definitions became famous in their own right: "Oats: A grain, which in England is generally given to horses, but in Scotland supports the people."

events.title: Pride and Prejudice Published
events.blurb: A 37-year-old unmarried English rector's daughter living quietly with her widowed mother in Hampshire published, anonymously, her second novel — a comedy of manners about five daughters of a small landowner, an arrogant wealthy suitor, and a perceptive heroine who misreads them both. The first edition of 1,500 copies was a modest success; the author made £140 from it. She would die four years later; her anonymity was preserved until a posthumous edition named her.
events.revealBlurb: January 28, 1813 — Jane Austen, attributed to "By the Author of Sense and Sensibility." She sold the copyright outright for £110; her estate never profited further. Austen is now the most continuously read English novelist. A first edition sold at auction in 2008 for £105,000.

events.title: Ulysses Published
events.blurb: An English-language bookshop owner in Paris published a 730-page Irish novel by a 40-year-old expatriate author that had been serialized, banned, confiscated, and partially burned in the United States. The book followed a single day — June 16, 1904 — in the lives of two Dublin men, using stream-of-consciousness narration that shifted style dozens of times across its 18 chapters. The American mail service seized copies until 1934.
events.revealBlurb: February 2, 1922 — James Joyce, 40th birthday; published by Sylvia Beach at Shakespeare and Company, Paris. The setting day — known as "Bloomsday" — is celebrated by Joyceans every June 16 with readings, pub crawls, and costumed reenactments.

events.title: Shays' Rebellion: Armed Farmers Storm Springfield Armory
events.blurb: A force of roughly 1,500 debt-ridden Massachusetts farmers led by Revolutionary War veteran Daniel Shays marched on the federal arsenal at Springfield in the depths of winter, hoping to seize weapons and overthrow a state government that was seizing their farms for unpaid taxes. State militia repelled the attack with cannon fire, killing four rebels — but the uprising terrified the nation's leaders into convening the Philadelphia Convention that produced the Constitution.
events.revealBlurb: January 25, 1787 — Springfield, Massachusetts. Daniel Shays was never caught and was eventually pardoned. George Washington, alarmed by news of the rebellion at his Mount Vernon retirement, came out of retirement to preside over the Constitutional Convention it helped cause.

events.title: President Kennedy Assassinated in Dallas
events.blurb: At approximately 12:30 pm that day, President John F. Kennedy was shot in the head while riding in an open motorcade through Dealey Plaza in Dallas, Texas, and was pronounced dead at Parkland Memorial Hospital at 1:00 pm. Lee Harvey Oswald was arrested that afternoon; two days later, Oswald was shot and killed on live national television by nightclub owner Jack Ruby before he could stand trial.
events.revealBlurb: November 22, 1963 — Dallas, Texas. Lyndon Johnson was sworn in as president on Air Force One, with a blood-spattered Jacqueline Kennedy standing beside him. The Warren Commission concluded Oswald acted alone; roughly 60% of Americans have never believed it.

events.title: Apollo 1 Launchpad Fire
events.blurb: During a ground test at Cape Kennedy that afternoon, a fire broke out inside the Apollo 1 command module, killing all three crew members — Gus Grissom, Ed White, and Roger Chaffee — in less than a minute. The cause was an electrical spark in an atmosphere of pure oxygen at elevated pressure, and the hatch could not be opened quickly enough to save anyone.
events.revealBlurb: January 27, 1967 — Launch Complex 34, Cape Kennedy, Florida. The crew could not escape because the hatch required 90 seconds to open inward — and the fire created pressure that made it impossible to swing. The disaster set the Moon program back 20 months but ultimately produced a safer spacecraft.

events.title: Reagan: "Tear Down This Wall"
events.blurb: Standing 100 yards from the concrete barrier dividing East and West Berlin that afternoon, President Ronald Reagan delivered a speech at the Brandenburg Gate in which he directly challenged Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev: "Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall!" His own State Department and National Security Council had urged him to remove the line as counterproductively provocative; Reagan insisted on keeping it.
events.revealBlurb: June 12, 1987 — Brandenburg Gate, West Berlin. At the time, the speech received relatively little media coverage and was dismissed as Cold War posturing by Soviet state media. Two years, four months, and 27 days later, the wall fell.

events.title: U.S. Invades Iraq
events.blurb: A U.S.-led coalition launched air strikes and a ground invasion of Iraq in a "shock and awe" campaign code-named Operation Iraqi Freedom, premised on intelligence assessments — later found to be wrong — that Saddam Hussein possessed weapons of mass destruction. The initial combat phase lasted 41 days; the subsequent occupation and insurgency lasted until 2011 and killed more than 4,400 American service members.
events.revealBlurb: March 20, 2003 — Baghdad, Iraq. No weapons of mass destruction were found. Saddam Hussein was captured hiding in a hole near Tikrit in December 2003 and executed by hanging in December 2006. President Bush declared "Mission Accomplished" on May 1, 2003, from the deck of an aircraft carrier; the war continued for eight more years.

events.title: Strange Fruit Recorded
events.blurb: A 23-year-old African-American singer, in a Manhattan studio, recorded a song about the lynching of Black Americans that had been written by a Jewish high-school teacher from the Bronx. Her regular label refused to release it; a tiny specialty label agreed. She closed with it at every set at her Greenwich Village club, the room going dark except for a spotlight on her face, no encore permitted. The song haunted her for the rest of her short life.
events.revealBlurb: April 20, 1939 — Billie Holiday, Commodore Records. Songwriter: Abel Meeropol, under the pen name Lewis Allan. Meeropol and his wife later adopted the two young sons of the executed Ethel and Julius Rosenberg.

events.title: Kind of Blue Released
events.blurb: A 33-year-old trumpet player released a five-track album recorded in two half-day sessions in a converted Manhattan church. He had given the musicians — including a young tenor saxophonist he had just hired — only short modal sketches, not written music, and one of the tracks was a single take. The album would become the best-selling jazz record of all time, its influence extending to rock, classical minimalism, and film scoring.
events.revealBlurb: August 17, 1959 — Miles Davis at 30th Street Studio, NYC. Sidemen: John Coltrane, Cannonball Adderley, Bill Evans, Paul Chambers, Jimmy Cobb. It has sold over 5 million copies in the US alone, received quintuple-platinum status.

events.title: Beatles' Final Public Performance
events.blurb: A four-piece rock band performed without announcement on the roof of their recording company's London headquarters for 42 minutes in near-freezing winter temperatures, drawing a crowd of hundreds in the street below before police ended the show citing noise complaints. The impromptu rooftop set was their last performance together in front of a live audience.

events.title: Live Aid
events.blurb: Two simultaneous 16-hour benefit concerts, one at a stadium in London and one at a stadium in Philadelphia, were broadcast live to an estimated 1.9 billion people in 150 countries — at the time perhaps 40 percent of the world population. The concerts raised around $127 million for Ethiopian famine relief. A British band's 21-minute set, by most accounts, stole the whole day. Its lead singer's synchronized clap-along with 72,000 people is the stuff of legend.
events.revealBlurb: July 13, 1985 — Wembley Stadium and JFK Stadium. The stealing-the-show band was Queen, Freddie Mercury at Wembley. Co-organizers Bob Geldof and Midge Ure. "Feed the World" had been launched by the Band Aid charity single the previous Christmas.

events.title: Spotify Launches
events.blurb: A Swedish music-streaming service, developed in Stockholm and Stockholm alone for two years, launched invitation-only to users in six European countries. The service offered an enormous music library — eventually over 100 million tracks — free with ads or $10/month without. It would restructure the entire music business: album sales collapsed, streaming became the default, and royalties flowed through aggregation models that artists found miserly.
events.revealBlurb: October 7, 2008 — founded by Daniel Ek and Martin Lorentzon. The service arrived in the U.S. in July 2011 after lengthy negotiations with major labels. It had 620 million monthly active users as of 2024 — the largest audio subscription service ever.

events.title: Pong Released in Arcades
events.blurb: A black-and-white rectangle containing two paddles and a bouncing dot was installed in a Sunnyvale, California tavern as a hardware test. The test machine broke within days — not from malfunction, but because the coin slot had overflowed with quarters. Atari scrambled to ship units nationwide, and the commercial video game industry was born.
events.revealBlurb: November 29, 1972 — Atari Inc., founded that June by Nolan Bushnell and Ted Dabney, shipped Pong to arcades. The Andy Capp's Tavern prototype jammed after a week because it held too many coins.

events.title: Pac-Man Debuts in Japanese Arcades
events.blurb: A yellow circle eating dots and fleeing ghosts through a maze seemed like a peculiar bet in an era dominated by shoot-'em-ups. It became the highest-grossing arcade game ever made, the first video game character to achieve mass-market celebrity, and the template for an entirely new genre. Its creator wanted a game that women would actually want to play.
events.revealBlurb: May 22, 1980 — Namco's Puck-Man (renamed Pac-Man for Western markets to prevent vandalism) went on location test in Shibuya, Tokyo. By 1982 an estimated 30 billion quarters had been inserted into Pac-Man machines worldwide.

events.title: Doom Uploaded to the Internet
events.blurb: At midnight, id Software attempted to upload its new game to a university FTP server. So many people were already waiting that the network collapsed. When the file finally went live, 10,000 simultaneous downloads crashed it again. Doom popularised the first-person shooter genre, the shareware distribution model, online multiplayer, user-generated mods, and the moral panic about video game violence — all within a few months.
events.revealBlurb: December 10, 1993 — id Software uploaded Doom to an FTP server at the University of Wisconsin–Madison after working 30 consecutive hours. The game sold over 2 million retail copies and was installed on an estimated 10 million PCs via shareware by 1995.

events.title: Final Fantasy VII Released in Japan
events.blurb: A Japanese role-playing game with pre-rendered 3D backgrounds, full orchestral-style music, and a story involving ecological collapse and corporate villainy sold out PlayStation consoles across Japan before it even launched. On release day it sold 1.75 million copies in a single country in a single day.
events.revealBlurb: January 31, 1997 — Final Fantasy VII launched in Japan for PlayStation. It sold 2.3 million copies in its first three days and over 6 million by 1998. Its western release September 7, 1997, introduced the JRPG genre to millions. The 2020 remake sold over 7 million copies in under four days.

events.title: The Sims Released
events.blurb: A game in which you build a house and manage the life of a simulated person — feeding them, making them use the bathroom, watching them catch fire if left unattended too long — became the best-selling PC game of the year, and then 2001, and then the best-selling PC game of all time. More than half its players were women, permanently disproving every assumption the games industry held about its audience.
events.revealBlurb: February 4, 2000 — Maxis and EA released The Sims for Windows. It sold 1.77 million copies in North America in its first year. The Sims overtook Myst to become the best-selling PC game ever in 2002. The franchise has sold over 70 million copies.
